title: Embedded notebook with live figures: can I read the derivation and run it?
summary: A mock-up of a notebook page: a short derivation, the code cell that makes the figure, the figure itself and a note on reproducibility. It teaches you to read a notebook as an argument: text, code and output are three parts of one claim.

media.alt: Mock-up of a notebook page with a derivation, a code cell, a decay plot comparing the exact solution with an Euler curve, and a reproducibility checklist.

read_the_figure.question: Can I read the derivation and run it?
read_the_figure.axes: The page: a header bar (notebook.ipynb, kernel idle, Run all); a text cell with the derivation; a code cell labelled In [1]; a figure (t in s from 0 to 5, u from 0 to 1) with exact and step 0.3 curves; a Reproducibility box with four rules.
look_at: What does the text claim, and does the code compute exactly that?
Do the code parameters match the figure? (the cell says dt = 0.1, the figure shows a step of 0.3)
What makes the notebook reproducible: seed, environment, run order?
What are the controls (Run all, kernel state)?
read_the_figure.proves: It lets a reader check the claim by re-running the code: if the same code gives the same figure, the result is reproduced. It does not prove the claim is true, only that it follows from the code.
if_wrong: Output that does not match the code above it (stale output).
No seed or environment: the figure may differ on another machine.
Cells that must be run out of order: the notebook is not reproducible top to bottom.

terms.meaning: A document that mixes text, code and the output of the code.
The process that runs the code; its state (variables) is what a cell result depends on.
One block of text or code; code cells have an In [n] number and an Out.
The starting value of a random number generator, fixed so that random results can be repeated.
A recorded set of package versions, so the code runs the same way later.

remember: Run top to bottom: the notebook must give the same figure.
Fix the seed and pin the versions.
The text, the code and the figure must agree on parameters.
Stale output is the commonest error.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The notebook uses three kinds of block: formatted text for the derivation, a code cell with an In [n] label in teal, and a figure placed beside as its output. Colour separates the roles (teal code, amber reproducibility). The header bar encodes state: kernel idle and the Run all control. The figure legends say what each curve is.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A derivation, the code and the result are three views of one argument, and a notebook puts them next to each other so each can be checked against the others. Live means the reader can change a cell and see the figure change, which is the way to test understanding. The reproducibility box says what the author did to make the check meaningful.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What does the derivation claim? That du/dt = -lambda u gives u = u0 exp(-lambda t) and that explicit Euler is stable when |1 - lambda dt| < 1. Q2: Does the code match the figure? The cell sets lam = 2 and dt = 0.1, and plots the exact exponential; the figure shows the exact curve and a step-0.3 Euler curve whose first point is 0.4 = 1 - 2 x 0.3 at t = 0.3, so the figure uses dt = 0.3, not 0.1. Q3: Is the step stable and accurate? |1 - 2 x 0.3| = 0.4 < 1: stable, but it falls faster than the exact solution (0.4 against e^(-0.6) = 0.55 at t = 0.3).

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Reproducible: seed fixed, environment pinned, top-to-bottom run. A notebook that cannot be re-run to give the same figure is a picture of a result, not evidence.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The figure may not come from the code shown: in this mock-up the cell sets dt = 0.1 while the figure shows a step of 0.3, so either the output is stale or the code is not the one that made it. Hidden state, cells run out of order and unpinned packages make results differ. A neat notebook may hide dead ends and failed runs. Interactive notebooks invite exploration but tempt a reader to trust the last output.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A script with a test suite (reproducible by command) is stricter than a notebook; a paper figure with a data file and a script is simpler; a Markdown report with code in an appendix; a workflow manager for long pipelines.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a cell that prints the library versions and the seed, a test cell that asserts the numerical value, and a fixed order of cells numbered from 1.

steps.title: Exact solution and the explicit Euler step
steps.tex: \dot u=-\lambda u\ \Rightarrow\ u(t)=u_0e^{-\lambda t},\qquad u_{n+1}=(1-\lambda\Delta t)\,u_n

steps.title: Stability and the first step
steps.note: For lambda = 2: the limit is dt = 1.0; with dt = 0.3 the first step is already 27 percent low.

worked.title: Check the notebook's claim for dt = 0.3
worked.problem: lambda = 2. Is explicit Euler stable for dt = 0.3? What are u after one and two steps, and the exact values?
worked.answer: Stable (factor 0.4); but the Euler values 0.40 and 0.16 are 27 and 47 percent below the exact 0.55 and 0.30.

create: Add the versions, the seed and one assert to the notebook, then run it top to bottom in a fresh kernel.
Convert the notebook into a script plus a figure file and compare what is lost.

checks.q: Why run a notebook top to bottom?
checks.answer: So that results do not depend on hidden state from earlier or out-of-order cells.

checks.q: lambda = 5. Largest stable explicit Euler step?
The output figure shows dt = 0.3 while the code shows 0.1. What are the possible explanations?
checks.hint: Stale output, edited code, other kernel state.
checks.answer: The output is stale (code edited after running), or the figure came from another cell or a previous kernel state; re-run in a fresh kernel and compare.
